meta.chapterLabel: Lesson 6: Going Places (1): Where Are You Going?

items.note: Same polite set as あちら (achira, 'over there', Lesson 5) and どちら (dochira, 'where', Lesson 1). Careful with こちら (kochira): so far this book teaches it only as 'this is …' for introducing a person (Lesson 1), not as a place.

The こちら (kochira) here is directional — 'this way' — not the 'this is …' introduction sense taught in Lesson 1. Said by a host showing you in; へ (e) marks the direction, as on its own card in this lesson.
items.reviewNote: Pulled forward from Lesson 9, where the book teaches it as this exact set phrase. Added so the directional sense of こちら is learnable alongside そちら／あちら／どちら rather than waiting.

items.hint: the usual choice of the two
items.note: Marks the destination of a motion verb like いきます (ikimasu, 'go') or きます (kimasu, 'come'), e.g. ぎんこうにいきます (ginkou ni ikimasu), 'go to the bank'. This lesson's へ (e) is interchangeable with に (ni) in this role — see that card. Same kana as the number に (ni, '2') from Lesson 2.
items.reviewNote: Possibly already taught — already introduced in Lesson 2: Possession: Whose Pen Is This? (matched on target)

items.note: Always used from the speaker's point of view: いきます (ikimasu) means moving away from where the speaker currently is, even when talking about going to where the listener is. Contrast きます (kimasu) 'come', which means moving toward the speaker's current location.
items.reviewNote: Possibly premature — explicitly taught later in Lesson 7: Going Places (2): I’m Going by Shinkansen (explicitly re-taught as a dedicated vocabulary/Key-Sentence item ("スミスさんは しんかんせんで おおさかに いきます"))

items.note: Comes at the end of a sentence or phrase to seek confirmation, spoken with rising intonation (like English 'isn't it?'). Spoken with falling intonation (sometimes lengthened to ねえ (nee)) it instead expresses admiration, agreement, or empathy.
items.reviewNote: Possibly premature — explicitly taught later in Lesson 9: Doing Things (2): Do You Often Come Here? (explicitly re-taught as its own dedicated vocabulary entry)
Added to demonstrate the confirmation-seeking particle ね (ne) in use — the chapter only shows it inside the skipped TARGET DIALOGUE, so this reuses that same line as a standalone example.
items.target: かいぎは１じからですね

items.note: ひとり (hitori, 'one person', an irregular counting word) + で (de) here marks a state or manner ('alone'), a different job from the で (de) in Lesson 4 that marked means or method (カードで, kaado de, 'by credit card').
Always used from the speaker's point of view: きます (kimasu) means moving toward where the speaker currently is. Contrast いきます (ikimasu) 'go', which is used even for going to where the listener is.

This と (to) means 'with, together with' before a motion verb, e.g. ともだちといきます (tomodachi to ikimasu), 'go with a friend' — a different job from the と (to) in Lesson 4, which only connects nouns as 'and' (カレーとサラダ, karee to sarada, 'curry and salad').
More formal, fuller form of じゃ (ja) from Lesson 4 — both mean 'well then', but じゃ is the casual contraction. This では (dewa) is also the base that じゃありません (ja arimasen, Lesson 2) contracts from.

Used as 'good-bye' when hanging up the phone or leaving a house or room. The same phrase しつれいします (shitsurei shimasu) is also used when entering a house or room, passing in front of someone, or leaving in the middle of a gathering, where it means 'Excuse me.'
items.reviewNote: Possibly already taught — already introduced in Frequently Used Expressions (matched on target) | Possibly premature — explicitly taught later in Lesson 7: Going Places (2): I’m Going by Shinkansen (explicitly re-taught as its own vocabulary entry, but re-glossed there as "Excuse me." rather than "Good bye." — worth the reviewer's eye given the differing sense taught)

items.english: Smith-san is going to the bank tomorrow.
items.target: スミスさんはあしたぎんこうにいきます

items.note: First of a three-way time prefix: せん〜 (sen-, 'last'), こん〜 (kon-, 'this'), らい〜 (rai-, 'next'), here + しゅう (shuu, 'week') — the same prefixes regularly build こんげつ／らいげつ (kongetsu/raigetsu, 'this/next month'), but not the year words (see きょねん, kyonen).
Past tense of いきます (ikimasu): ます (masu) → ました (mashita), the same ending swap as です (desu) → でした (deshita) in Lesson 2.

items.english: Smith-san went to Osaka last week.
items.target: スミスさんはせんしゅうおおさかにいきました

items.note: Extends the day words from Lesson 3: おととい (ototoi, 'day before yesterday') → きのう (kinou, 'yesterday') → きょう (kyou, 'today') → あした (ashita, 'tomorrow') → あさって (asatte, 'day after tomorrow').
items.reviewNote: Possibly premature — explicitly taught later in Lesson 8: Doing Things (1): I’m Going to Eat Tempura (explicitly re-taught as a dedicated Key Sentence item (recurs again in ch. 30's Key Sentences too))

items.english: Smith-san went to a restaurant with a friend yesterday.
items.target: スミスさんはきのうともだちとレストランにいきました

items.note: Breaks this lesson's せん／こん／らい pattern: きょねん (kyonen, 'last year'), ことし (kotoshi, 'this year'), and らいねん (rainen, 'next year') don't follow the regular せんげつ／こんげつ／らいげつ (sengetsu/kongetsu/raigetsu) pattern used for weeks and months.
Attaches to the place of departure. どこから きましたか (doko kara kimashita ka), 'Where did you come from?', is often understood as asking for someone's country of origin when asked of a non-Japanese person.

items.note: Past tense of きます (kimasu), formed the same way as いきました (ikimashita, see that card): ます (masu) → ました (mashita).

items.english: Smith-san came from the United States last year.

items.english: Smith-san, will you go to Kyoto tomorrow?

items.note: いきません (ikimasen) is the negative present of いきます (ikimasu): ます (masu) → ません (masen), the verb counterpart of です (desu) → じゃありません (ja arimasen) from Lesson 2.

items.english: Smith-san is going to the party.
items.note: Shows that the particle へ (pronounced え) can substitute for に after a place/event noun with motion verbs like いきます (ikimasu).
items.target: スミスさんはパーティーに／へいきます

items.english: (particle expressing apposition — 'X who is a Y')
items.note: Here の (no) marks apposition, not possession or affiliation — インターンの ラジャさん (intaan no Raja-san) means 'Raja-san, who is the intern', not 'the intern's Raja-san'.
items.reviewNote: Possibly already taught — already introduced in Lesson 1: Meeting: Nice to Meet You (matched on target)
Added to demonstrate apposition の (no) in a standalone sentence, reusing the chapter's own dialogue line since it otherwise only appears inside the skipped TARGET DIALOGUE/SPEAKING PRACTICE scripts.
items.target: こちらはインターンのラジャさんです

items.note: Optional — Japanese nouns don't normally pluralize on their own; たち (tachi) explicitly marks a group and attaches only to words for people, e.g. ともだちたち (tomodachitachi, 'friends'), not to objects.
items.reviewNote: Written 〜たち in the source

items.english: I'm going to the park with (my) friends.
items.reviewNote: Added to demonstrate the plural suffix たち (tachi) in a standalone sentence, reusing vocabulary already introduced in this chapter since none of the chapter's extractable sentences use it.
items.target: ともだちたちとこうえんにいきます

items.note: どれ (dore) is used alone to mean 'which one'; どの (dono) is used instead when 'which' is followed by a noun, e.g. どの バス (dono basu) 'which bus'.
が (ga) replaces the topic marker は (wa) after interrogatives like どれ (dore) or どの…(dono...), and is repeated in the answer to such a question.

items.scene: picking out which one of several, as in a だれが (dare ga) question

items.note: Suffix — attaches after a number to label something by its position or number, e.g. 6ばん (roku-ban) 'No. 6'.
